source.title: Revisiting the Volume Hypothesis
source.authors: Ari Pakman; Lior Kreimer; Yakir Berchenko

record.file_problem: Full paper text supplied, including results and appendices.
record.tranche_reason: The study uses Replica Exchange Wang–Landau density estimates to compare interpolating networks found by random sampling with gradient-trained networks. This conceptually tests whether typical interpolating solutions approach gradient-learning performance as training data grow; its binary-weight models and measurements differ from the cited Guess-and-Check and modern continuous-weight experiments.
record.gate_note: The study estimates test accuracy for zero-training-error binary networks under random sampling and reports GD/SGD comparisons. It does not test fitting random labels, or the claim versions' specified model families and recipes. Values used only to tune sampling and figure-only density-curve details are not separate rows.
record.test_reason: The study tests the volume hypothesis, which none of V1–V8 states. Its width comparisons concern typical randomly sampled binary interpolating networks or gradient-trained networks without reported training error or convergence. They do not establish V2's improvement from widening gradient-trained networks beyond the width needed to fit. Random weights are not random labels; density-curve curvature is not magnitude-aware sharpness; and both full-batch and minibatch training use Adam.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate: the authors conclude that gradient training's advantage over typical random interpolating solutions generally diminishes with increasing data, and interpret optimization and architectural biases as complementary, data-dependent mechanisms. This is a trend within moderate-scale binary networks, not demonstrated equality with gradient training or monotonic gap reduction in every condition.
record.recipe_differences: Uses binary-weight networks and Replica Exchange Wang–Landau density estimates to locate typical interpolating solutions, then compares them with Binary Connect GD/SGD using Adam; it is not the cited continuous-weight Guess-and-Check method.
record.method_sensitivity: Training-set size changes the random-sampling versus gradient-training accuracy gap; architecture and dataset also change the reported accuracies. The authors report that density curves sharpen with larger training sets.

fits_no_version.finding: Typical randomly sampled zero-training-error binary networks have lower test accuracy than both gradient comparators in every Table 2 configuration. The advantage generally shrinks with more data, but does not decline monotonically in every configuration.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: For these binary networks, the performance advantage of gradient training over typical random interpolating solutions generally decreases as training-set size increases.

fits_no_version.finding: Doubling the fully connected hidden width raises typical random-interpolator accuracy in five of six dataset-size conditions; Fashion-MNIST with 300 examples changes from 62.1% to 62.0%. Gradient-trained wider models have higher mean accuracy in all six conditions, but their training errors are unreported.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Increasing hidden width in these binary convolutional architectures generally improves test accuracy under random interpolation sampling and Binary Connect training.

record.peer_reviewed: Proceedings of the 43rd International Conference on Machine Learning, Seoul, South Korea. PMLR 306, 2026.
record.problems: The authors restrict experiments to binary-weight, moderate-scale architectures on MNIST and Fashion-MNIST with training sets of 30, 300, or 600. The test accuracy density is estimated over restricted accuracy ranges and the estimates vary across runs (Figure 2); the table reports uncertainty for GD/SGD, but not random-sampling maxima.
record.rows_left_out: No Table 2 rows omitted. Figure-only density curves in Figures 3–4 and curve variability in Figure 2 are not transcribed as additional numerical rows.

untested.parts: Random-label fitting capacity and natural-versus-random-label held-out performance under the same recipe.
Continued test-error improvement when widening gradient-trained networks past a demonstrated zero-training-error threshold; convergence and training errors are not reported.
Convolutional versus fully connected architectures and the contribution of local connectivity.
Adaptive versus nonadaptive optimizers and sensitivity to tuning; both reported gradient methods use Adam.
Large-batch penalties under fixed epoch budgets and adaptations that remove them.
Dropout interventions and their dependence on dataset size or augmentation.
Magnitude-aware perturbation sharpness, its association with train–test gaps, and comparisons with other measures.
Removing memorized examples versus randomly selected examples and retraining.

record.verdict_notes: All Table 2 accuracies, uncertainties, model sizes, and stated minibatch sizes match the supplied text. The rows are valid performance measurements, but their observed states cannot be interpreted as observations of V1–V8. Figure-only density concentration is already declared in rows_left_out and does not measure V7.

versions.untested_parts: Does not train on fixed random labels or compare held-out accuracy for random versus natural labels under the same architecture and recipe.

Does not test one-hidden-layer ReLU networks widening beyond the interpolation threshold under the specified standard gradient-training setup; wider architectures here are binary-weight convolutional networks.
Does not compare convolutional and fully connected networks on the specified image datasets or examine learned local connections.
Does not compare adaptive optimizers with SGD across the specified benchmarks and tuning regimes; its gradient-training comparison uses Binary Connect with Adam.
Does not vary batch size or study large-batch training under epoch budgets.
Does not add or remove dropout.
Does not measure magnitude-aware sharpness or compare it with norm- and margin-based measures.
Does not remove memorized training examples or retrain after removal.
